slides.title: Title
slides.notes: Open by reminding students that ordinary conjugacy already turns convex functions into families of supporting affine certificates. This section asks for the same idea in saddle form, where one variable is convex and the other is concave. The biconjugate check is the anchor for whether the transform kept the right information.

slides.title: Saddle Pairing
slides.notes: Do not rush the sign convention. In a saddle function, x and y have opposite geometric roles. The conjugate transform has to remember which variable is minimized and which one is maximized. That is why a naive two-variable convex conjugate would lose the saddle interpretation.

slides.title: Inverse Bifunction
slides.notes: Use this slide to make the inverse bifunction feel like a controlled coordinate change. It is not just swapping two letters. The reversal must preserve which direction is convex and which direction is concave, because the later minimax conclusions depend on the orientation of the two optimization variables.

slides.title: Quadratic Saddle
slides.notes: Introduce the quadratic as the section's laboratory. It is not meant to replace the theorem, but it exposes the moving pieces. Students can evaluate the saddle, transform it, transform it back, and compare sampled values. That makes biconjugacy a visible reconstruction property.

slides.title: Biconjugate Reconstruction
slides.notes: Connect this theorem with earlier convex biconjugacy. The second transform does not magically preserve every poorly behaved expression. It recovers the correctly closed saddle object. That closure warning is central because minimax equalities can fail when boundary or existence information is lost.

slides.title: Minimax Theorem Route
slides.notes: Use this slide as the theorem roadmap. The program is encoded as a saddle object, transformed through conjugacy, and compared after closure. Equality of values is one conclusion, while the actual existence of a saddle point is a stronger statement that needs attainment hypotheses.

slides.title: Existence Conditions
slides.notes: Clarify the difference between proving equality of values and proving that a saddle point exists. Compactness, level control, and closure are all ways of preventing limiting certificates from drifting out of the problem. Students should name which existence mechanism is being used.

slides.title: Numerical Checker
slides.notes: Tie the slide directly to the notebook invariant. The computation transforms the saddle and then reconstructs it. The grid residual is not the full theorem, but it is an excellent guard against sign mistakes, orientation errors, and missing closure operations in the synthetic example.

slides.title: Learner Lab
slides.notes: Frame the lab as a transform audit. Students should perturb the saddle, perform the conjugate operation, reconstruct with the biconjugate, and compare values. If the residual grows, the explanation should identify whether the issue is sign orientation, domain restriction, or a missing closure condition.

slides.title: Recap
slides.notes: Close by reinforcing the workflow. First orient the saddle variables correctly. Then apply the signed conjugacy transform and check biconjugate reconstruction. Finally use closure and existence hypotheses to turn the transform information into minimax equality and, when possible, an attained saddle point.
